h1: Sorghum and other grains for gluten-free beer
title: Sorghum and Gluten-Free Grains for Beer | Craft Beer School
desc: How to brew gluten-free beer with sorghum, millets and rice: gelatinisation, enzymes, yeast nutrition and keeping gluten out of the plant.
teaser: Sorghum can make a properly good lager. It just will not do it the way barley does. Here is how to brew gluten-free beer on a commercial kit.
standfirst: Gluten-free beer is a different process, not a barley recipe with a grain swapped in. Sorghum, millets and rice each bring their own problems with starch, enzymes and yeast food. The plant has to keep gluten out from intake to packaging.
sections: Gluten free and gluten reduced are different products

A gluten-free beer is made from grains that contain no gluten: sorghum, rice, maize, millets and pseudocereals like buckwheat. A gluten-reduced beer is brewed from barley and treated with an enzyme, usually a proline-specific endoprotease, that breaks gluten fragments down. We cover that route in how enzymes are used to make gluten-reduced beer.

The distinction matters for labelling. Internationally, the Codex Alimentarius standard sets 20 mg/kg of gluten as the ceiling for a gluten-free claim. Indian labelling rules come from FSSAI and change from time to time, so check the current regulation before you print a claim on a can. Testing gluten in fermented beer is also harder than in bread, because standard tests struggle with broken-down protein fragments.

Sorghum (jowar in most of India) is the most proven base for gluten-free beer. Sorghum lagers have been brewed commercially in Africa for decades. It is drought tolerant, widely grown in Maharashtra and Karnataka and cheap compared with imported malt.

Its problem is starch. Sorghum starch gelatinises at around 70 to 80 °C, well above the 62 to 72 °C range where barley amylases do their work. Malted sorghum also tends to have low diastatic power, especially low beta-amylase. So a sorghum mash with no help converts poorly and leaves a thin, starchy wort.
Cook the grain then add enzymes

Most commercial gluten-free brewers solve this in one of two ways. The simplest is to buy converted sorghum syrup or extract and build the beer on that. The other is to brew from whole grain:

  1. Cook milled sorghum or rice in a cereal cooker with a heat-stable alpha-amylase, holding near boiling for 20 to 30 minutes to gelatinise and liquefy the starch.
  2. Cool to around 60 to 65 °C and add a saccharifying enzyme such as a glucoamylase or a beta-amylase preparation.
  3. Add a glucanase if the mash is viscous.

The enzyme supplier's data sheet sets the dose and temperatures, so follow it. Our guide to exogenous enzymes in high adjunct brewing goes deeper on the same tools.
Millets and rice fill the gaps

Sorghum on its own can taste slightly sour or metallic. Many brewers blend it. Rice lightens the body and flavour. Finger millet (ragi) and pearl millet (bajra) add colour and an earthy grain character. India grows all of them at scale, which is a real advantage. Toasting or lightly roasting millet in a dry pan or a coffee roaster gives darker beers some colour without barley.

Without husk, these grains make a poor filter bed. Rice hulls are naturally gluten free and are the standard fix. Use flaked or torrefied forms where you can, as our guide to flaked grains explains, to skip some of the cooking.
Feed the yeast because sorghum wort is short of nitrogen

Barley wort carries plenty of free amino nitrogen (FAN) for yeast growth. Sorghum and rice worts carry much less. Low FAN gives slow, sulphury fermentations that can stall. Plan for it:

  • Add a complete yeast nutrient with zinc and amino nitrogen, not just diammonium phosphate.
  • Pitch generously, around 1 million cells per ml per degree Plato for an ale.
  • Oxygenate well at the start.

Check your yeast and any fining agents are gluten free too. Most dried brewing yeast is grown on molasses, but the supplier should confirm it in writing.
Keep barley out of the plant

The hardest part of a gluten-free line in a working brewery is cross-contact. Malt dust travels. One shared hose or a mash tun with a film of barley protein can push a batch over the limit. Brewers who do this seriously run a separate mill or clean the mill thoroughly, brew gluten-free batches after a full clean-in-place (CIP) cycle and test finished beer before release.

Writing that control plan, choosing an enzyme programme and sizing the yeast nutrient is a process design job. It draws on mash chemistry, yeast physiology and quality systems at once. A guide can show the route but cannot walk you through it for your plant.
Bitterness and finish need a lighter hand

Gluten-free beers often taste thinner than barley beers at the same gravity. Barley brings proteins and dextrins that round out the palate. Sorghum and rice worts carry less of both. A hop bill that tastes balanced in your barley lager can feel harsh in a sorghum version. Many brewers trim bitterness by 10 to 20% on their first gluten-free batch and add body with a slightly higher saccharification temperature or a share of unfermentable dextrin.

Carbonation helps too. Around 2.6 volumes of CO2 lifts aroma and makes a lighter body feel livelier on the tongue.

Before you commit a full brew, run a 20 litre pilot on sorghum syrup with 20% cooked rice, a good nutrient and a clean ale yeast. Send a sample for gluten testing and taste it blind against your house lager. That one pilot tells you whether to chase the grain route or stay with syrup.
faqs: Sorghum contains no gluten, so a beer brewed only from sorghum and other gluten-free ingredients can be gluten free. Cross-contact in a shared brewery is the usual risk.
Sorghum starch gelatinises at around 70 to 80 °C and malted sorghum is low in beta-amylase. Brewers cook the grain and add commercial enzymes to convert it.
Can I use millets in gluten-free beer?
Yes. Finger millet and pearl millet work well blended with sorghum or rice. Toasted millet adds colour and an earthy grain note.
What is the gluten-free limit for beer?
The international Codex standard is 20 mg/kg. Indian rules come from FSSAI and change, so check the current regulation before making a label claim.
